messages.subject: syntax and crash re ./
parts:
I have been using and proseltyzing Stan for 3 years. Stan is great and keeps getting better.
The following simple model to fit a diminishing returns curve compiles with stan_model:

data{

    int        N;

  vector[N]  X;

  vector[N]  Y;

}

parameters{

real<lower=0> Prod; # slope at origin 

  real<lower=0> Cap;  # asymptote

real<lower=0> sigma; # SD of lognormal residuals

}

model{

# internal variables

vector[N] Yfit; # predicted Y

# prior distributions.     

Prod ~ gamma(2.0,0.05); # mode at 20.0

   Cap  ~ gamma(2.0,0.2); # mode at 5.0

sigma~ gamma(2.0,2.0); # mode at 0.5

# prediction and likelihood

Yfit <- X ./ (1.0/Prod + X / Cap);

  Y ~ lognormal(log(Yfit), sigma);

}

But, shouldn't this model should throw a syntax error?    X / Cap  is [vector] / [real] so it should be
        Yfit <- X ./ (1.0/Prod + X  ./ Cap);
according to Stan 2.9.0 manual page 356:

                vector operator./(vector x, real y) The elementwise quotient of y and x.


Here is the fun part.  When coded as X ./ Cap,  I do not get a syntax error, I get a spectacular, 500 line report about mysterious crashes.
Here is the not-fun part. That report suggests missing libraries, which sent me on a wild goose chase before I tracked this down to a dot.
Attached is the sessionInfo() report (latest everything).  Also attached is the world's worst error message.

Can you straighten me out here?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] syntax and crash re ./
parts:
Thanks for the reproducible bug report.

There's nothing wrong with

> Yfit <- X ./ (1.0 / Prod + X / Cap);


because we have these signatures:

operator/(vector, real) : vector

operator+(real, vector) : vector

But there is a bug in the Stan code generator for this:

> Yfit <- X ./ (1.0 / Prod + X ./ Cap);

Whenever the C++ fails to compile, it's a bug on our
end. I filed an issue and assigned it to myself for 2.10:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1883

When it's fixed, (X ./ Cap) will produce the same value
as (X / Cap), so you can just go with the latter for now.

- Bob
